children.text: OneCare Vermont was founded in 2013 by the University of Vermont Medical Center and Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center as a shared Accountable Care Organization vehicle. It became the lead entity under Vermont's federal All-Payer ACO Model, a Total Cost of Care arrangement intended to align Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers under a single accountability framework — the first statewide model of its kind in the U.S. OneCare Vermont wound down its operations at the close of 2025, twelve years after founding; the federal all-payer agreement that defined its most consequential years ran about eight of those years before its own scheduled sunset.

OneCare Vermont served as the ACO responsible for managing care for attributed beneficiaries across participating payers, using prospective capitation for Medicaid and shared savings for Medicare, with commercial contracts varying by plan. At its broadest, participation reached all fourteen Vermont hospitals and thousands of providers. Participation itself, however, was voluntary rather than mandated for every payer — a design choice with structural consequences covered below.
The Policy Constraint: Why “Voluntary” Had Teeth

In 2016, the U.S. Supreme Court decided Gobeille v. Liberty Mutual Insurance Co., 6–2, holding that ERISA preempts state laws requiring health plans — including self-insured employer plans — to report claims data into a state's all-payer claims database. The practical effect: Vermont could not compel every private payer into its data and payment infrastructure. That limit became concrete on January 1, 2023, when Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont — the state's largest insurer — declined to renew its OneCare contract, removing roughly 93,000 enrollees, about a third of OneCare's total enrollment, in a single step. Blue Cross cited inadequate contractual protection for its members' claims data under a plan to subcontract analytics to UVM Health Network (a competitor), and no evidence among its own members of progress on health outcomes or cost of care.

The financial record is genuinely contested, not a clean success or failure, and any summary that offers a single tidy number should be treated with suspicion. OneCare's administrative costs ran $70.35 million from 2018 through 2022. One projection found the ACO's total cost of care ran $42.28 million higher than a no-ACO counterfactual over the period studied — $89.56 million higher excluding the pandemic-distorted year. Vermont's State Auditor separately found more than $25 million in additional spending on ACO operations from 2017 through 2020 compared with traditional fee-for-service. Other analyses point the other way: one calculation found $18.23 million in net savings, though excluding 2020 from that same calculation flips it to a $32.38 million cost; a Medicaid-specific measure found $21.43 million in savings under that program alone.

On utilization, the State Auditor's 2021 report found that Vermonters attributed to OneCare visited the emergency department at a rate roughly 36% higher than peer ACOs nationally and had about 18% fewer primary care visits — the signature of a population managed reactively rather than proactively. A 2019 audit separately found OneCare "did not reliably monitor or accurately report" several community-based programs it had funded, producing no evidence of results from those investments.

Vermont's experience is most useful read as a specific, documented mechanism rather than a generic caution about "voluntary programs." Three lessons hold up: (1) a state cannot assume it can compel every private payer's participation — federal ERISA preemption is a real, binding constraint on how far any state mandate can legally reach, as Gobeille v. Liberty Mutual demonstrated; (2) real-time analytics need to precede the assumption of downside financial risk, not follow it — OneCare's own staff acknowledged to state regulators that its analytics lagged newer available systems; and (3) "savings" claims for a total-cost-of-care model are highly sensitive to which years and cost categories are included, so expect a genuinely contested verdict rather than a clean one. Vermont's legislative response, Act 68 of 2025, makes reference-based pricing and hospital global budgets mandatory for all Vermont hospitals — closing the hospital-side version of this gap, though it has no power to override the federal, payer-side constraint that Gobeille established.

metrics: Wound down at the close of 2025, after 12 years (2013–2025)
BCBS Vermont exit (Jan. 2023) removed ~93,000 enrollees — about a third of total enrollment
Financial verdict contested: one analysis found $18.23M in savings; excluding 2020, the same method shows a $32.38M cost
36% higher ED visit rate than peer ACOs nationally (VT State Auditor, 2021)
summary: OneCare Vermont operated the first statewide all-payer ACO in the U.S. from 2013 until winding down at the close of 2025. Its record is genuinely contested — a documented Policy-pillar constraint (Gobeille v. Liberty Mutual) let the state's largest insurer exit in 2023, and independent financial analyses reach conflicting conclusions on net savings vs. net cost.
title: Vermont's All-Payer ACO: A Twelve-Year Test of Voluntary, Total-Cost-of-Care Reform
